title: Virtual slices and oversubscription governor proposal
body:
Summary:

This doc proposes a "virtual slices" abstraction plus an "oversubscription governor" that together let Redwood Dedicated offer higher utilization without sacrificing tenant-level predictability. Goal is to give product and ops a levers-based system to: 1) guarantee baseline latency and throughput for committed slices, 2) opportunistically pack surplus capacity across pools, and 3) gracefully degrade tenants that exceed their entitlement while preserving core SLOs.

Context / motivation:
- Customers want predictable throughput for bursty applications but we observe a lot of idle GPU time at night and uneven utilization across pools.
- Existing approaches (hard isolated pools, ad-hoc burst credits) either waste capacity or cause noisy neighbor pain when oversubscribed.
- We need a middle path: deterministic guarantees for committed units and controlled best-effort usage on top.

Definition: virtual slice
- A named allocation object representing a tenant's logical share on a given Dedicated pool.
- Properties: slice_id, committed_rps (or tokens/sec equivalence), max_soft_rps, priority_tier, preemption_policy, metrics_tags.
- A slice is not necessarily tied to a fixed number of GPUs; it maps into runtime concurrency targets and token-rate budgets enforced by the request broker.

Definition: oversubscription governor
- A cluster-level controller that tracks real-time headroom and makes binary decisions about admitting soft (best-effort) work beyond committed slices.
- Inputs: per-instance GPU utilization, queue latency percentiles, active slice budgets, pending best-effort queue size, global headroom budget per pool.
- Outputs: per-slice admission rate, temporary elevated budgets for opportunistic tenants, and preemption signals when headroom falls.

Design goals (ranked):
1) Preserve committed slice SLOs (p50/p95 latency targets, throughput floors).
2) Increase GPU utilization without adding tail latency to guaranteed tenants.
3) Make oversubscription predictable and auditable for billing.
4) Operational simplicity: runbook, observability, back-pressure hooks.

Admission/Enforcement model:
- Each slice has two rate budgets: committed_budget and soft_budget. committed_budget enforces contractual throughput via token-bucket on the request broker path.
- soft_budget is a tunable multiple (e.g., up to 2x) allowed when governor gives permission. Soft requests are labeled; they can be throttled or preempted without violating committed budgets.
- Governor computes pool headroom = sum(pool_capacity) - estimated_committed_demand - safety_margin. If headroom > threshold, allow soft budgets proportionally to tenant weights.
- Preemption: If pool headroom drops below critical, governor issues preemption notices to the broker to drain soft requests from lowest-priority slices first. Preemption policy: warn (N seconds), then immediate drop or migrate to fallback model.

Heuristics and scoring:
- To decide who gets opportunistic capacity, governor uses a scoring function combining: recent slice utilization (prefers those under-utilizing committed budget), tenant-tier weight, billing sensitivity (customers marked as opportunistic), and historical fairness score.
- Example score = w1*(1 - committed_utilization_ratio) + w2*tier_weight + w3*(1 - soft_usage_last_10m)
- Tunables: w1,w2,w3 set by product; default w2 >> w1 to prefer tiered commercial commitments.

Operational signals and metrics to track:
- Per-slice: committed_throughput, soft_throughput, commited_p95_latency, soft_p95_latency, preemptions_count, soft_drop_rate.
- Pool-level: gpu_utilization, headroom_bytes (or tokens), queue_length, preemption_events, time_to_recover_after_burst.
- SLOs: committed tenants must maintain p95 <= target and <1% request error attributable to preemption.

Billing and metering implications:
- Bill committed_budget as contract units (monthly/annual).
- Bill soft usage as discounted metered units with separate line item. Need clarity: is soft usage guaranteed where billed? Recommend soft usage is always best-effort and billed at lower rate with explicit terms.

Failure modes and graceful degradation:
- Governors lagging or crash: safe default -> enforce only committed budgets until controller recovers. This is conservative but prevents noisy neighbor issues.
- Overaggressive admission -> increased tail latency for committed tenants. Mitigation: conservative safety_margin and better signals (queue latency + kernel-level telemetry).

Runbook (operational playbook):
- Alerting: when pool_headroom < safety_threshold -> P1 page to SRE; when committed_slo_breaches increase by 3x rolling 5m -> SRE + Product Pager.
- Emergency mitigation: automated snapshot -> reduce all soft_budgets by 50% and throttle new soft admissions for 2m, then resume gradual ramp.
- Scaling: if headroom persistently < target for >30m, recommend auto-provision additional nodes or move tenants to other pools via migration schedule.

Rollout plan (phases):
Phase 0 (sim): run governor in read-only mode producing admission recommendations and alerts for 2 weeks against historical traffic to validate scoring function.
Phase 1 (opt-in beta): select 5 customers (mix of tiers) to opt-in to soft capacity in a single pool; enable soft billing lines; monitor SLOs + fill. 2 weeks.
Phase 2 (controlled ramp): enable governor-driven soft admission across 3 pools with auto-fallback rules; tune weights and preemption timings. 4 weeks.
Phase 3 (GA): enable on all non-sensitive pools; add features: per-tenant soft budgets UI, analytics, and SLA language updates.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How to map slice committed_rps to runtime concurrency and token budgets for different model sizes? (Need mapping table per model family.)
- Can we allow multi-pool spanning slices (elastic slices) to increase reliability? Complexity vs benefit.
- Billing: what discounts to offer for soft usage while keeping economic incentives aligned?
- Security: how to ensure soft requests from one tenant cannot amplify performance issues for others (kernel isolation and scheduler checks)?

Next steps / action items:
- Engineering: prototype governor read-only simulator (owner: Evan) by 2025-01-24, include historical replay harness.
- Applied-ML: propose default rps->concurrency mapping per model family (owner: Lina) by 2025-01-28.
- PM/Product ops: draft customer-facing beta terms and pricing for soft usage (owner: Priya) by 2025-02-07.
- SRE: add metrics + dashboards (owner: Ravi) by 2025-02-03.

Notes / rough thoughts (informal):
- I like the concept because it gives a clean separation: committed units are sacrosanct, everything else is a citizen-of-the-pool. Helps conversations with sales: "you get guaranteed throughput + opportunistic capacity at discount".
- We should be careful about naming; "oversubscription" sounds risky to customers. Consider marketing name: "burst sharing" or "elastic slices".
- We will need a small audit trail recording when governor allowed soft capacity and which tenants were preempted; important for billing disputes.

References:
- Related tickets: DED-4201 (burst credits analysis), DED-3983 (tenant isolation metrics), GOV-102 (resource controller prototype).
- Slack discussion: #dedicated-capacity thread on 2024-12-17 (see pinned messages).

This doc is a draft; comments welcome. Priorities for the next meeting: agree on scoring defaults and the conservative safety_margin (suggested start: 20% of pool capacity).
